title: 376. Geometry, Spatial Thinking & Measurement: Parallel and Perpendicular Line Slopes
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a slope parallel to a given nonvertical line.
questions.question: What is the slope of any line parallel to \(y=4x-7\)?
questions.explanation: Parallel nonvertical lines have equal slopes. The given line has slope \(4\).
questions.hint: Compare the directions of parallel lines.

questions.learningObjective: Find a slope perpendicular to a given nonhorizontal line.
questions.question: What is the slope of a line perpendicular to \(y=-3x+2\)?
questions.explanation: Perpendicular finite slopes satisfy \(m_1m_2=-1\). Thus \((-3)m_2=-1\), giving \(m_2=\frac{1}{3}\).
questions.hint: Include both the reciprocal and the sign change.

questions.learningObjective: Recover a line's slope before finding a parallel slope.
questions.question: What is the slope of a line parallel to \(2x+5y=10\)?
questions.explanation: Rearranging gives \(y=-\frac{2}{5}x+2\). A parallel line has the same slope, \(-\frac{2}{5}\).
questions.hint: Isolate the vertical coordinate before reading the slope.

questions.learningObjective: Convert standard form and compute a perpendicular slope.
questions.question: What is the slope of a line perpendicular to \(6x-2y=1\)?
questions.explanation: The equation becomes \(y=3x-\frac{1}{2}\), with slope \(3\). Its perpendicular slope is \(-\frac{1}{3}\).
questions.hint: Determine the original slope before taking its negative reciprocal.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the slope of a line perpendicular to a vertical line.
questions.question: What is the slope of a line perpendicular to \(x=7\)?
questions.explanation: The given line is vertical. A perpendicular line is horizontal and has slope \(0\).
questions.hint: Use the horizontal-vertical relationship rather than a reciprocal of an undefined value.

questions.learningObjective: Identify the slope behavior of a perpendicular vertical line.
questions.question: What is the slope of a line perpendicular to \(y=-4\)?
questions.explanation: The given line is horizontal. Any perpendicular line is vertical, whose slope is undefined.
questions.hint: Identify the direction of the perpendicular line.

questions.learningObjective: Compute a two-point slope and transfer it to a parallel line.
questions.question: What is the slope of a line parallel to the line through \((-2,1)\) and \((2,7)\)?
questions.explanation: The original slope is \(\frac{7-1}{2-(-2)}=\frac{6}{4}=\frac{3}{2}\). A parallel line retains this slope.
questions.hint: Find the rise and run of the original line first.

questions.learningObjective: Use a slope product to classify two lines.
questions.question: Two lines have slopes \(\frac{2}{5}\) and \(-\frac{5}{2}\). Which relationship holds?
questions.explanation: Their slope product is \(-1\), so the lines are perpendicular. Their slopes are unequal, so they are not parallel.
questions.hint: Compare both the slopes and their product.

questions.learningObjective: Recover a coordinate from a perpendicular-slope condition.
questions.question: The line through \((1,2)\) and \((4,k)\) is perpendicular to a line of slope \(-\frac{1}{2}\). What is \(k\)?
questions.explanation: The required slope is \(2\). Thus \(\frac{k-2}{3}=2\), giving \(k=8\).
questions.hint: Find the required slope before using the two-point formula.

questions.learningObjective: Solve a coefficient using a perpendicular-slope product.
questions.question: The lines \(ax+2y=8\) and \(3x-6y=2\) are perpendicular. What is \(a\)?
questions.explanation: Their slopes are \(-\frac{a}{2}\) and \(\frac{1}{2}\). The product condition gives \(-\frac{a}{4}=-1\), hence \(a=4\).
questions.hint: Express each slope in terms of its standard-form coefficients.
